skill.name: wordpress-router
skill.description: Classifies WordPress repositories and routes plugin, theme, block, core, and site tasks to the right workflow.
skill.summary: Route WordPress repository work to the correct workflow after project triage.
skill.author: Automattic

security_audit.summary: The static findings are markdown code-span matches rather than Ruby or shell backtick execution. The skill documents local WordPress triage and routing steps, with no evidence of prompt injection, data exfiltration, or malicious intent.

finding_verdicts.reason: Line 25 is markdown inline code documenting a hardcoded local triage command. It does not use shell interpolation or user-controlled arguments.
Line 32 is a markdown reference to a local decision-tree document. It is not executable code and does not invoke a shell.
Line 44 uses inline code formatting for the literal triage value kind: unknown. There is no command execution behavior.
Line 45 lists local file and directory names in markdown code spans. These references are inspection targets, not shell commands.

content.value_statement: WordPress repos can mix plugins, themes, core, and site code, which makes task routing slow. This skill classifies the repo and directs the agent to the right WordPress workflow and guardrails.
actual_capabilities: Runs a documented WordPress project triage command to detect repo kind and tooling.
Classifies plugins, themes, block themes, WordPress core checkouts, Gutenberg repos, and site repos.
Routes work by user intent to relevant WordPress domain workflows.
Lists guardrails for version constraints, existing tooling, and repository conventions.
Recommends rerunning triage and using existing lint, test, and build commands after changes.
limitations: Requires a repository root and a clear user intent to route accurately.
Depends on the separate WordPress project triage script being available.
Some target workflows are marked as planned rather than fully implemented.
Does not make WordPress changes by itself; it selects the right workflow first.

use_cases.title: Start Plugin Maintenance
use_cases.description: Classify a plugin repository, identify available tooling, and route admin, hooks, REST, or security tasks.

use_cases.title: Prepare Theme Work
use_cases.description: Determine whether a theme uses classic templates or block theme files before editing templates or theme.json.

use_cases.title: Triage Mixed Site Repos
use_cases.description: Route full site repositories where plugin, theme, and wp-content changes may overlap.

prompt_templates.title: Classify a Repository
prompt_templates.prompt: Use wordpress-router in this repository. Classify the project type, list detected tooling, and tell me which workflow should handle the task.

prompt_templates.title: Route Plugin Work
prompt_templates.prompt: Use wordpress-router for this WordPress plugin. I need to add an admin settings page, so identify the right workflow and checks first.

prompt_templates.title: Plan Theme Changes
prompt_templates.prompt: Use wordpress-router on this theme repository. Target WordPress 6.9 and PHP 8.1, then route block theme or classic theme changes.

prompt_templates.title: Resolve Mixed Routing
prompt_templates.prompt: Use wordpress-router on this full site repo. Inspect the triage result, route mixed plugin and theme work, and define verification commands.

output_examples.input: A user asks for a Gutenberg block bug fix in an unknown WordPress repo.
output_examples.output: The skill identifies a block plugin, routes to block development, and recommends existing build and test commands.

output_examples.input: A user asks to change theme styles in a repository with theme.json and templates.
output_examples.output: The skill routes to block theme work and calls out version constraints before edits begin.

output_examples.input: A user opens a large wp-content repository and asks for performance improvements.
output_examples.output: The skill treats it as a full site repo, routes by performance intent, and narrows the likely scan scope.

best_practices: Run routing before making WordPress code changes in unfamiliar repositories.
Confirm WordPress and PHP version targets when the repository does not show them.
Use the repository's existing lint, test, and build scripts after routed changes.
anti_patterns: Do not assume every wp-content repository is only a plugin or only a theme.
Do not skip version constraints when routing core, theme, or plugin work.
Do not invent verification commands when the repository already provides scripts.

faq.question: What does wordpress-router do?
faq.answer: It classifies WordPress repositories and routes work to the most relevant WordPress workflow.

faq.question: Does it edit WordPress code directly?
faq.answer: No. It helps choose the correct workflow and guardrails before implementation begins.

faq.question: Which repository types can it identify?
faq.answer: It covers plugins, mu-plugins, themes, block themes, WordPress core, Gutenberg, and full site repos.

faq.question: Does it require WP-CLI?
faq.answer: Some downstream workflows may require WP-CLI, but the router first checks available tooling.

faq.question: Can it handle ambiguous repositories?
faq.answer: Yes. It asks one clarifying question when the repository kind or user intent remains ambiguous.

faq.question: Which AI tools support this skill?
faq.answer: The report lists support for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code.
